subject: Cooking
title: The Bread Tax: When Bread Was Taxed by Weight
description: One-minute skill: The Bread Tax: When Bread Was Taxed by Weight.

hook.text: For 600 years in England, bread prices were set by law. Bakers who cheated faced the pillory.

buildup.text: The Assize of Bread (1266) fixed bread weight and price relative to wheat cost — consumer protection law.

discovery.text: Bakers added a 13th loaf to every dozen — the 'baker's dozen' — as insurance against being accused of shorting.

twist.text: The Corn Laws (1815–1846) kept grain prices artificially high to benefit landowners — workers starved.

climax.text: Repealing the Corn Laws was Britain's biggest free-trade victory, making bread affordable for the working class.

punchline.text: The phrase 'baker's dozen' is a 750-year-old fear of punishment.

quiz.question: Why did bakers add a 13th loaf to a dozen?
options: To avoid punishment for selling underweight bread

details.summary: For centuries, governments regulated bread through Assize of Bread laws that fixed the weight a loaf must contain for a given price. English laws dating to 1266 tied baker profits to grain prices, with punishments including fines and pillory.
details.whyItMatters: Bread taxation reveals how seriously governments treated bread as essential infrastructure. These regulations were among history's earliest consumer protection laws.
takeaways: England's Assize of Bread dates to 1266 and regulated loaf weight
Bakers gave thirteen for a dozen to avoid underweight penalties
Bread regulation was among the earliest consumer protection laws

faq.question: What penalties did bakers face for underweight bread?
faq.answer: Penalties varied by era and severity. Fines were common. Repeat offenders could be placed in the pillory, publicly shamed, or banned from baking. The severity reflects how seriously authorities treated bread fraud when bread was the primary food of the poor.

faq.question: Why is a baker's dozen thirteen instead of twelve?
faq.answer: Bakers added an extra loaf when selling a dozen to ensure the total weight met or exceeded legal requirements. Getting caught selling underweight bread meant severe punishment. The extra loaf was insurance against the variability of hand-shaped dough before standardized pans.
